newsitem.title: CHAD: Low turnout in Chad legislative poll runoff.
newsitem.headline: Low turnout in Chad legislative poll runoff.

text.p: People in Chad on Sunday appeared to be staying away from polling stations for the parliamentary runoffs, apparently because of the belief that the president's party was assured victory.

Polling stations in the 11 constituencies in the capital N'Djamena where reruns were taking place were largely deserted after polls opened at 6 a.m. Election officials and state radio reported a similar trend in the interior.
Both the opposition and the ruling party called for a high turnout in the polls for 68 seats.
Many voters blamed the apparent lack of enthusiasm on the fact that victory for President Idris Deby's party looked pretty much a foregone conclusion.

"People are discouraged and estimate that victory is practically guaranteed for the ruling party which was overwhelmingly ahead in the first round," one voter told state radio in the southern commercial town of Moundou.
Deby and his supporters need to get at least 26 seats in the runoff to ensure a majority in the new 125-member parliament.
Final results from the January 5 first round released by the appeal court credited Deby's Patriotic Salvation Movement with 37 seats against a total of 20 for various other parties.

The runoff, like the main poll, is widely expected to show massive support for Deby in the capital and the rest of the largely Moslem north. His opponents hold sway in the predominantly Christian or animist south.
The head of the Independent National Electoral Commission CENI called on Saturday for the authorities to remain neutral.

CENI head Pascal Yoadimnadji said in a statement broadcast on state radio and television that the country's administration, army and traditional chiefs should not interfere in polling -- "on pain of scrapping of results".
Deby, a former guerrilla leader from the Moslem north, seized power in a 1990 French-backed coup after decades of civil war or conflict with Libya.
After repeated electoral delays, he won a multi-party presidential election in July in a runoff against fellow general Wadal Abdelkader Kamougue from the largely Christian south.
Chad, a sprawling former French colony on the fringes of the Sahara desert, previously had a 57-member interim assembly under a 1993 transitional charter.
The appeal court scrapped votes cast by many of the country's nomads in the first round of the parliamentary poll.
The nomad vote was a source of dispute during last year's presidential election, with the opposition denouncing multiple or under-age voting.
Polls were scheduled to close at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT) with vote counting starting immediately in the presence of polling agents of parties and candidates.
Past experience suggests it could be several days before the first results are out.
